facts.statement: Glacialisaurus was a sauropodomorph dinosaur that lived in Antarctica during the Early Jurassic period.
facts.quote: Glacialisaurus is a genus of sauropodomorph dinosaur from the Early Jurassic period of Antarctica.

facts.statement: The fossils date to the Pliensbachian stage of the Early Jurassic, approximately 186 to 182 million years ago.
facts.quote: They come from sedimentary rocks of the Hanson Formation and date to the Pliensbachian stage of the Early Jurassic, around 186 to 182 million years ago.

facts.statement: The genus is known from two specimens: a partial tarsus and metatarsus, and a partial left femur.
facts.quote: It is known from two specimens; the holotype (name-bearing specimen), a partial tarsus (ankle) and metatarsus, and a partial left femur (thigh bone).

facts.statement: The species was formally described and named in 2007.
facts.quote: The fossils were described in 2007, and made the basis of the new genus and species Glacialisaurus hammeri.

facts.statement: The fossils were found in the lower Hanson Formation of Mount Kirkpatrick in the Central Transantarctic Mountains.
facts.quote: Fossils of a sauropodomorph dinosaur were discovered by a field team from Augustana College led by paleontologist William R. Hammer during 1990–91 fieldwork in the lower Hanson Formation of Mount Kirkpatrick in the Central Transantarctic Mountains of Antarctica, dating to the Early Jurassic.

facts.statement: The fossils were sent to the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago and first reported in 1994.
facts.quote: The fossils were sent to the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago, USA, and were first reported in 1994.

facts.statement: Nathan Smith and Diego Pol described the genus and species, naming the holotype specimen FMNH PR1823.
facts.quote: The fossils were described by the paleontologists Nathan Smith and Diego Pol, who named the new genus and species Glacialisaurus hammeri, with FMNH PR1823 as holotype specimen.

facts.statement: The genus name combines the Latin word for 'icy' with the Greek word for 'lizard'.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from the Latin root glacialis meaning icy after its discovery in the Beardmore Glacier region in the Central Transantarctic Mountains and the word sauros meaning lizard.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus is classified as a massospondylid, a group of basal sauropodomorphs.
facts.quote: This dinosaur has been classified as a massospondylid, a group of medium-sized, basal (early diverging or "primitive") sauropodomorphs that existed during the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic on every continent except Australia.

facts.statement: The estimated total length of Glacialisaurus is 6.2 meters.
facts.quote: Its length has been estimated at 6.2 m.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus was a large herbivore, though average in size for its group.
facts.quote: Glacialisaurus was a large herbivorous dinosaur, though it was average sized for a massospondylid.

facts.statement: As a basal sauropodomorph, it likely had a long neck, a small head, and leaf-shaped teeth.
facts.quote: As a basal sauropodomorph, Glacialisaurus would have had a long neck and a proportionally small head with leaf-shaped teeth.

facts.statement: Its hand was short, wide, and robust, featuring a large claw on the thumb.
facts.quote: The hand would have been short, wide, and robust with a large claw on the thumb.

facts.statement: It possessed a robust medial epicondylar crest on the femur, a trait convergently evolved in basal theropods.
facts.quote: The medial epicondylar crest extends from the medial surface of the lower femoral shaft and is distinct from all other sauropodomorphs in that it is robust, a trait convergently evolved in basal theropods.

facts.statement: The first metatarsal was roughly three-quarters the length of the second metatarsal.
facts.quote: Metatarsal I is roughly 3/4 the length of metatarsal II, as in most basal sauropodomorphs.

facts.statement: The second metatarsal features a weakly convex front border, a hypertrophied lateral plantar flange, and a robust medial distal condyle.
facts.quote: The diagnostic traits (characteristics that distinguish a taxon from others) of the second metatarsals include: a front border that is weakly convex in proximal aspect; a hypertrophied lateral plantar flange on the proximal end (present, but less developed in many basal sauropodomorphs, e.g., Saturnalia, Plateosaurus); and a medial distal condyle that is more robust and well−developed than the lateral distal condyle.

facts.statement: Fossils of Cryolophosaurus, a pterosaur, and a tritylodont were found at the same site at an elevation of about 4100 meters.
facts.quote: Several other fossils were collected from the same site, including fossils of the carnivorous theropod dinosaur Cryolophosaurus, a pterosaur humerus (upper arm bone), and a large tooth of a tritylodont, all found at an elevation of about 4100 m.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus is frequently classified as a member of the Massospondylidae family, a group of non-eusauropod sauropodomorphs that lived from the Late Triassic to the Early Jurassic across multiple continents.
facts.quote: Massospondylids are a group of non-eusauropod sauropodomorphs that existed during the Late Triassic to Early Jurassic in Africa, Antarctica, Asia, and the Americas.

facts.statement: Smith and Pol identified Glacialisaurus as a massospondylid in their 2007 phylogenetic analysis.
facts.quote: In their 2007 phylogenetic analysis of the relationships of Glacialisaurus, Smith and Pol found that it was a massospondylid.

facts.statement: The genus Glacialisaurus was named by Smith and Pol in 2007.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Smith & Pol, 2007

facts.statement: The species Glacialisaurus hammeri was named by Smith and Pol in 2007.
facts.quote: species_authority: Smith & Pol, 2007

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus was approximately 8 meters long from head to tail and weighed between 4 and 6 tonnes.
facts.quote: Glacialisaurus fue un sauropodomorfo que medía aproximadamente 8 metros de cola a cabeza y que pesaba de 4 a 6 toneladas.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus is a robust non-eusauropod sauropodomorph characterized by a robust distal epicondylar border on the femur.
facts.quote: Glacialisaurus es un robusto sauropodomorfo no eusaurópodo que se caracteriza por un borde robusto epicondilar en distal del fémur

facts.statement: The second metatarsal of Glacialisaurus features a convex proximal border and a hypertrophied lateral plantar phalanx at the distal end.
facts.quote: el segundo metatarsiano con un borde convexo en proximal, falange lateral plantar hipertrofiada en distal del metatarsal II

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus lived during the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stages of the Early Jurassic, approximately 194 to 188 million years ago.
facts.quote: The specimens were discovered in tuffaceous siltstone deposited in the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian stage of the Early Jurassic, dating to about 194–188 million years ago.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus lived in Antarctica during the Early Jurassic, approximately 190 million years ago.
facts.quote: que vivió a principios del período Jurásico, hace aproximadamente 190 million years ago, en el Sinemuriano, en la Antártida.

facts.statement: The time range for Glacialisaurus is recorded as the Sinemurian to Pliensbachian, from 199.5 to 184.2 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Sinemurian to Pliensbachian (199.5 to 184.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus inhabited forests of large trees covering the then temperate Antarctica.
facts.quote: Habitaba en un bosque de grandes árboles que cubría la entonces templada Antártida.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus lived on the coast of a river flowing into the sea of the supercontinent Gondwana during the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: Vivió durante el Jurásico temprano era la costa de un río que desembocaba en el mar del supercontinente de Gondwana.

facts.statement: Remains of Glacialisaurus, including a femur, incomplete ankle, and feet, were found in the Southern Hemisphere summer of 1990–1991 by Hammer and a team at Mount Kirkpatrick in the Beardmore Glacier region of the Transantarctic Mountains.
facts.quote: Los restos de Glacialisaurus, un fémur, un tobillo incompleto y los pies, fue encontrado en el verano austral de 1990 a 1991 cuando Hammer y un equipo de investigadores encontraron los fósiles de ese dinosaurio en el Monte Kirkpatrick, en la región del Glaciar Beardmore en la Cordillera Transantártica, en la Formación Hanson.

facts.statement: The Glacialisaurus fossils remained unstudied for over ten years due to a lack of knowledge to interpret their identity.
facts.quote: Los materiales deben haber estado sin estudiar unos diez años o más, porque no existían los conocimientos para interpretar la identidad de esos restos.

facts.statement: The fossils underwent nearly three years of preparation and study by Diego Pol of CONICET and Nathan Smith of the University of Chicago.
facts.quote: Los fósiles estuvieron cerca de tres años en preparación y estudiados por Diego Pol, investigador del CONICET, quien actualmente trabaja en el Museo Paleontológico Egidio Feruglio, en Chubut, y por Nathan Smith, de la Universidad de Chicago.

facts.statement: The genus name Glacialisaurus derives from the Latin 'glacialis' meaning frozen or icy, referring to its location at the Beardmore Glacier, and the Greek 'saurus' meaning lizard.
facts.quote: El nombre del género proviene del Latín “glacialis” que significa congelado o helado por su localización, el Glaciar Beardmore y del griego “saurus” por lagarto.

facts.statement: The species name 'hammeri' honors Dr. William R. Hammer of Augustana College, a key promoter of Antarctic paleontology and the discoverer of the fossils.
facts.quote: La especie “hammeri” es en honor del Dr. William R. Hammer del Augustana College, uno de los principales impulsores de la paleontología antártica y descubridor de los fósiles.

facts.statement: Fossils of a sauropod found at the Beardmore Glacier in the same period as Glacialisaurus demonstrate that prosauropods and sauropods coexisted in the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: En el Glaciar Beardmore también se encontraron fósiles de un saurópodo que habitó ese lugar en el mismo período que el glacialisaurio, cosa que demuestra que los prosaurópodos y los saurópodos convivieron s principios del Jurásico.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus was found alongside Cryolophosaurus, a small pterosaur, a rat-sized synapsid called Tritylodon, and an unknown theropod.
facts.quote: Glacialisaurus fue encontrado junto a Cryolophosaurus, un pequeño pterosaurio, un Tritylodon (un sinápsido del tamaño de una rata), y un terópodo desconocido.

facts.statement: Fossilized tree trunks up to 2 meters high have been found in the same formation as Glacialisaurus.
facts.quote: También se han encontrado troncos fosilizados de 2 metros de alto.

facts.statement: The phylogenetic position of Glacialisaurus is considered unstable due to its fragmentary nature, though it is frequently recovered as a massospondylid.
facts.quote: The phylogenetic position of Glacialisaurus is unstable due to its fragmentary nature, but it is frequently found to be a member of the family Massospondylidae.

facts.statement: Glacialisaurus was found approximately 650 km from the South Pole, which was located about 1000 km farther north at the time.
facts.quote: Glacialisaurus was found about 650 km from the South Pole, which was about 1000 km or so farther north at the time.
